title: TANASE AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
summary:
In the case of Tanase and Others v. Romania, the applicants were 24 Romanian nationals of Roma origin, all formerly residents of the village of Bolintin Deal in Giurgiu County. Their case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma communities to collective violence and state inaction, focusing on the destruction of their homes and the long-term deprivation that followed. On the night of 6–7 April 1991, after a Roma individual killed a non-Roma villager, a large mob—encouraged by local officials—attacked Roma homes, burning and destroying over twenty houses and forcing the entire Roma community to flee. Further attacks occurred in May 1991 when Roma families attempted to return, resulting in additional homes being set alight. The authorities failed to protect the applicants’ property or ensure their safe return, and the Roma community remained displaced, facing ongoing discrimination, lack of legal residence, and denial of access to essential services.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The Court declared the case admissible, recognising the serious issues raised, but had not yet issued a final judgment on violations or remedies at the time of this decision.

This case is significant as it exposes the persistent risks of mob violence, forced displacement, and institutional neglect faced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe, reflecting a broader historical pattern of exclusion and discrimination that continues to demand robust legal protection.
